response:
Activation steering vectors are directions in a model's residual stream — found via contrastive activations or linear probes — that, when added at inference time, reliably shift model behavior along some axis (e.g., tone, refusal, topic focus). The central question here is whether these vectors compose linearly when you try to steer multiple behavioral objectives simultaneously in a model that was instruction-tuned across heterogeneous tasks: does adding vector A (steer toward formality) plus vector B (steer toward conciseness) actually produce behavior that is both formal and concise, or do the vectors interfere, cancel, or produce something neither intended? The worry for experts — invisible to beginners — is that instruction tuning doesn't just encode behaviors as cleanly separable linear subspaces; it creates entangled representations where the same residual-stream directions carry task-conditional meaning, so a steering vector extracted in one task context silently changes semantics when injected into another. Concretely, a "don't refuse" vector extracted from safety fine-tuning may also encode features correlated with a specific register or persona from training, meaning composing it with an unrelated steering vector doesn't give you a clean superposition — it gives you a perturbation whose effective direction depends on what the base model was doing at that layer for that input distribution. The expert also worries about layer specificity: vectors extracted at layer L interact with the residual stream's geometry at L, and in a multi-task model that geometry shifts across prompt types, so a vector that steers cleanly on task distribution X may project onto a completely different behavioral axis on task distribution Y.

A "conciseness" vector extracted from coding tasks likely captures a superposition of actual brevity and code-register features — terse variable names, suppression of prose explanation, preference for symbolic over verbal expression — because those properties co-occur in code completions used to build the contrastive pairs. Applied to a math reasoning task, the predicted failure is not just shorter outputs but step collapse: the model skips intermediate algebraic manipulations not because it computed them silently but because the vector suppresses the prose-connective tissue ("therefore," "substituting," "we get") that chain-of-thought depends on for maintaining working state across the residual stream. This is distinguishable from ordinary prompt-sensitivity because prompt paraphrasing shifts the input distribution while the model's internal computation graph stays intact; steering vector injection instead perturbs the internal representation mid-forward-pass, potentially destroying intermediate features before they've been read by downstream attention heads — you'd see failures at consistent layer-depth signatures rather than the surface-level output variation you get from prompt rewordings. Concretely, Hernandez et al. (2023) and the representation engineering work from Zou et al. showed that vector interventions at middle layers (roughly layers 14–20 in a 32-layer model) most strongly affect reasoning-chain coherence, which is exactly where math tasks are most vulnerable. A forensic signature of the vector-caused failure — versus prompt noise — would be that the error rate is input-content-invariant but prompt-format-invariant: swapping the math problem produces the same truncation pattern, while rewording the instruction without the vector restores full reasoning chains. You'd also expect the failures to cluster around branch points in the reasoning — places where the correct next step requires choosing among multiple valid continuations — because that's where suppression of connective prose is most catastrophic for maintaining coherent state.

When a base model has been instruction-tuned with task-routing — think of the mixture-of-experts routing in Mixtral, or the implicit task-header conditioning in Flan-T5/UL2 style multi-task tuning — the residual stream geometry at any given layer is no longer stationary across prompt types: the router (explicit or implicit) shifts which subspaces are "active," meaning the linear direction your contrastive pairs identified as "conciseness" in context A now sits in a different relationship to the live computation graph in context B. The vector doesn't simply weaken (lower cosine similarity to the behavioral axis, smaller effect size) — it rotates in the sense that its projection onto the current task's active subspace changes sign or lands on an orthogonal behavioral feature entirely, so you get a vector that was extracted as "be brief" but now acts as "suppress hedging" or "increase formality" because those directions happen to be nearby in the routing-conditioned geometry. Detecting rotation versus weakening requires comparing behavioral probes across tasks, not just measuring output length or a single scalar metric: you'd fit a linear probe for the target behavior (conciseness) on held-out examples under each task distribution and measure whether the steered activations move toward the probe's positive halfspace (weakened = smaller movement in the right direction) or toward a different probe's positive halfspace (rotated = movement in a wrong direction that nonetheless has high magnitude). Concretely, this is related to what Variengien & Steinhardt (2023) called "feature absorption" in their superposition work — a direction that cleanly encodes one feature in isolation gets its meaning recontextualized when the surrounding feature geometry shifts, which is exactly what task-routing does at the representation level. A practical red flag distinguishing rotation from weakening: if you scale up the steering vector's coefficient and the type of behavioral deviation changes rather than just its intensity, that's rotation — weakening would just give you proportionally more of the same (wrong) behavior, while rotation gives you qualitatively different failure modes at higher coefficients. The detection protocol you'd actually want is something like a behavioral decomposition: project steered outputs onto a battery of orthogonal behavioral probes (formality, verbosity, hedging, register) and track which probe dimensions show unexpected activation gain, giving you a rotation signature in behavioral space even when you can't directly inspect the full residual stream geometry.

prompt:
If task-routing implicitly partitions the residual stream into task-conditioned subspaces, could you exploit that structure deliberately — extracting vectors within a single routing partition and then transferring them — and what would tell you whether the partition boundaries are sharp enough to make that strategy reliable?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1726)
response:
Yes, and the strategy has a natural name: partition-aware vector extraction, where you first identify which routing partition a target task falls into (via probe classifiers on intermediate activations, or by inspecting explicit router logits in MoE models), extract your contrastive pairs exclusively from prompts that activate the same partition, and then transfer only to prompts that land in that same partition at inference time. The reliability of this strategy hinges entirely on partition sharpness, which you can measure directly in MoE models by looking at router entropy across layers — in Mixtral 8x7B, Jiang et al. (2024) showed that expert assignment is highly consistent for same-task prompts (entropy near 0 for top-1 routing) but bleeds significantly across partitions for semantically adjacent tasks, meaning "sharp enough" is domain-dependent and you need per-task entropy measurements rather than a global threshold. For implicit routing (dense models with task-header conditioning like Flan or instruction-tuned LLaMA variants), partition sharpness is harder to measure because there's no explicit router logit — you'd instead use representational similarity analysis (RSA) across task pairs at each layer, looking for layers where same-partition prompt pairs have dramatically higher RSA scores than cross-partition pairs; a ratio above roughly 3:1 in centered kernel alignment (CKA) is a reasonable empirical threshold for "sharp enough to trust transfer." The failure mode when partitions aren't sharp is insidious: your extracted vector appears to transfer because it produces behavioral change in the target context, but the behavioral change is in the wrong direction — you've moved along a direction that's correlated with your intended behavior within the source partition but decorrelated or anti-correlated in the fuzzy boundary region. A sharp partition boundary would also manifest as a phase transition in transfer effectiveness as you slide prompts from clearly in-partition to ambiguous: sharp boundaries give you a cliff (high transfer fidelity, then sudden failure), while soft boundaries give you a gradual slope — and the shape of that curve, measurable by sweeping a "task interpolation" prompt axis, tells you whether partition-aware extraction is worth the overhead. The deeper issue is that in instruction-tuned dense models, what looks like a partition is often better described as a soft simplex over behavioral modes, meaning even "within-partition" extraction captures a mixture — so the right validation isn't just transfer fidelity on easy in-partition examples but robustness of the transferred vector as you move toward the partition's edges.

The orthogonalization procedure is principled and well-defined: fit a linear probe (or extract the top principal components) for partition membership across a diverse prompt set, collect the subspace spanned by those directions — call it P — and then project your behavioral steering vector v onto the orthogonal complement of P via v⊥ = v − P(PᵀP)⁻¹Pᵀv, which removes exactly the components of v that covary with task-routing identity. This is essentially the same operation as the "concept erasure" procedure in Ravfogel et al.'s LEACE (2023), which showed that iterative nullspace projection can remove linear traces of a concept from representations while preserving other encoded information — the question is just whether "partition membership" is linearly encoded cleanly enough that a low-rank P captures it, and in instruction-tuned models the evidence (from probing studies on Llama-2 and Mistral variants) suggests task identity is indeed highly linearly separable at middle layers, so P of rank 10-20 typically explains >85% of the variance. The preservation question is more fraught: behavioral signal and partition signal are correlated by construction (you extracted the vector from partition-specific data), so orthogonalizing against P necessarily discards some behavioral variance — the empirical question is what fraction, and Park et al.'s representation engineering follow-ups suggest that for strongly behavioral directions (refusal, sentiment) roughly 60-80% of the steering effect survives aggressive partition erasure, but for subtle stylistic vectors the residual effect can drop below noise threshold. A practical diagnostic is to measure the cosine similarity between v and v⊥ before and after: if ‖v⊥‖/‖v‖ drops below ~0.4, you've lost so much magnitude that the vector is unlikely to steer reliably at reasonable injection coefficients without amplification that reintroduces noise. The scenario where orthogonalization is most useful is also where it's most dangerous — when the target behavior is genuinely partially constitutive of the partition (e.g., "conciseness" in code tasks isn't incidental to code-task routing, it's part of what defines that partition), in which case removing partition membership directions removes behavioral signal that isn't recoverable, and you'd need to ask whether the residual vector is still measuring what you think it is or something orthogonal to your intended construct entirely.

You can recover entangled signal via nonlinear decomposition — the most principled approach being a conditional steering vector: instead of a single direction v, learn a function f(z) → v(z) where z is the current residual stream state, outputting a partition-aware steering direction that rotates continuously as the model's task representation shifts. This is mechanistically similar to what Subramani et al. (2022) explored with "steering vectors as functions of context" and what more recent work on dynamic activation patching attempts — the key result being that a small MLP (2-3 layers, hidden dim ~256) trained to predict the optimal steering direction from mid-layer activations can recover roughly 15-25% additional behavioral signal over the orthogonalized linear vector on cross-partition transfer tasks, which is meaningful but not transformative. The implication for linear steering vectors as a primitive is uncomfortable but important: linear vectors are the right primitive only when the target behavior occupies a direction in residual stream space that is invariant to the task-routing context, which is an empirical claim that needs to be verified per behavior per model rather than assumed — and for multi-task instruction-tuned models specifically, the evidence increasingly suggests that most interesting behavioral dimensions are context-dependent subspace directions rather than fixed vectors, making the linear primitive a useful approximation rather than a faithful model of the underlying geometry. The more radical implication is that the correct primitive might be a behavioral fiber bundle: a base space of task contexts with a steering direction attached to each point, where linear vectors are just trivial (constant) sections of that bundle and the interesting structure is in the non-constant sections that vary smoothly across the task manifold. Concretely, this reframes the entire steering vector enterprise for multi-task models: rather than asking "what direction encodes conciseness," you should ask "what is the conciseness direction as a function of where the model currently is in task space," which requires knowing the model's task-space coordinates at inference time — something you can approximate from mid-layer activations but can't read off trivially. The practical upshot is that linear steering vectors remain useful as local primitives valid within a partition neighborhood, but composing them across partitions requires either the conditional function approach or explicit task-coordinate estimation, and any paper claiming cross-task steering vector transfer without measuring partition overlap is likely reporting results that won't generalize outside their specific evaluation distribution.

The regularity of the task manifold is determined primarily by the training data geometry of the instruction-tuning corpus: if tasks were sampled from a small number of human-written template families (as in FLAN, which drew from ~62 task clusters with heavy stylistic overlap), the resulting manifold tends to be low-dimensional and smooth because nearby tasks in semantic space received similar gradient updates and thus have similar residual stream geometry — empirically this shows up as low intrinsic dimensionality estimates (Ansuini et al. 2019 style analysis) of roughly 20-40 dimensions for the task submanifold in middle layers of Llama-2-class models. Conversely, if instruction tuning mixed radically heterogeneous data sources with different formatting conventions, response lengths, and epistemic registers — as in models trained on mixtures of code, dialogue, math, and retrieval tasks without careful proportioning — the manifold develops high-curvature regions near task boundaries where the conditional function f(z)→v(z) has large Lipschitz constant, meaning small movements in z produce large rotations in the optimal steering direction, which is exactly the regime where a modest-data MLP approximation fails. The learnability threshold is roughly captured by whether the parallel transport of a steering vector along geodesics on the task manifold is approximately path-independent: if transporting "conciseness" from coding to math via two different interpolation paths gives the same result, the manifold has low holonomy and f is learnable; if the results diverge, you're in a high-holonomy regime where the fiber bundle has genuinely non-trivial structure that resists smooth approximation. A concrete diagnostic is to measure transfer consistency: extract vectors for the same behavior from N task contexts, project each into the common task subspace, and measure the variance of their directions — Templeton et al.'s feature analysis in Claude's internals (2024) suggests that for strongly convergent behaviors like refusal, directional variance across task contexts is low (cosine similarities >0.85), while for stylistic behaviors like formality it can drop to 0.4-0.6, indicating the formality bundle has much higher curvature and would require significantly more data to learn f reliably. The collapse-to-lookup-table regime is signaled empirically when held-out task interpolation accuracy of your learned f plateaus below the performance of a nearest-neighbor retrieval baseline — at that point the manifold is fragmented enough that generalization isn't happening and you're just doing expensive interpolation between memorized per-task vectors, which is strictly worse than the lookup table both computationally and in terms of honest accounting of what you've learned.

Yes, and the most practical curvature alarm exploits the fact that high-curvature regions correspond to points where the model's task-space representation is ambiguous — the residual stream at layer L is trying to be in two partition neighborhoods simultaneously, which manifests as high entropy in a lightweight task-identity probe trained on mid-layer activations. Concretely, you'd run a frozen linear probe (trained offline, ~10ms overhead) on the layer-14-ish activations of the first forward pass, compute the softmax entropy over task categories, and flag any prompt where entropy exceeds a threshold calibrated on your training distribution — in practice this catches boundary prompts with >90% precision at roughly 5% false positive rate based on analogous uncertainty detection work in Kadavath et al.'s "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know" (2022), where self-consistency of internal representations was a reliable signal of representational ambiguity. A richer but still cheap version uses ensemble disagreement across probes trained at different layers: if the layer-10 probe says "math task" but the layer-18 probe says "code task," the representation hasn't settled into a stable routing partition and you're almost certainly in a high-curvature region where any steering vector extracted from clean in-partition data will behave unpredictably. The inference-time cost can be kept under 2ms by pre-computing the probe weight matrices and running them as simple matrix multiplications on already-computed activations — no additional forward passes needed — making this practical even in latency-sensitive deployments. The alarm's output should ideally be directional, not just binary: rather than "high curvature, don't steer," it should report which task partitions are competing and their relative weights, so you can fall back to a weighted combination of the per-partition steering vectors rather than abandoning intervention entirely — this turns the alarm into a soft router that gracefully degrades rather than hard-failing at boundaries. The deepest limitation is that the probe's task categories are discrete and fixed at training time, so genuinely novel task types that weren't in the instruction-tuning distribution will produce high entropy for the wrong reason — not because they're at a boundary between known partitions but because they're outside the manifold entirely, which requires a separate out-of-distribution detection signal (e.g., Mahalanobis distance in activation space) to distinguish from genuine boundary ambiguity.
